Snap Inc. is finalizing a settlement in a lawsuit filed by two teenagers who say years of compulsive scrolling and posting on the company’s photo-sharing app contributed to their mental health struggles, according to attorneys for the plaintiffs.
The agreement, reached partway through jury selection in Los Angeles, would enable the company to avoid the next high-profile social media addiction trial. The case in California state court was set to be the latest test of thousands of such lawsuits. The teenagers previously reached confidential settlements with Meta Platforms Inc., TikTok and Google’s YouTube.
“Our ultimate goal is to hold these social media companies accountable for how their actions have impacted millions of children across the country, and these settlements allow us to keep building toward that goal,” John Morgan and Emily Jeffcott, attorneys for one of the teens, said in a statement announcing the agreement. Terms of the settlement weren’t disclosed.
Related: As AI Laws Proliferate, Liability and Coverage Questions Multiply
The two cases, which were combined by the judge, would have been the second to go to trial among thousands of lawsuits filed by young users and their family members accusing the social media companies of engineering their platforms to profit at the expense of young people’s safety and mental health.
The companies deny these allegations and stress that they have rolled out tools and resources to support parents with teens on the platform. They’ve also sought to highlight positive experiences that users have online.
Snap didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
The teenage plaintiffs in the case that was scheduled to go to trial this week are identified in court documents as S.J., a 16-year-old girl from Illinois, and K.D.B., an 18-year-old woman from Mississippi. Both claim their heavy use of Snapchat and other social media platforms caused and contributed to their depression, anxiety and eating disorders.
Related: Meta Settles With Teen During Trial Testing Claims Social Media Caused Depression, Eating Disorders
Families shouldn’t have to seek jury trials “to solve a problem this big,” Mark Lanier, the plaintiffs’ trial counsel for the case, said in a statement. “What these teenagers need is a permanent fix, real design changes that protect kids, not case-by-case patches. Until that happens, we will keep trying these cases.”
S.J. and K.D.B.’s lawsuits were selected from the larger pool of litigation to serve as so-called bellwether cases. The outcomes of these early trials could encourage broader settlement talks by showing lawyers the strengths and weaknesses of their arguments and evidence — and ultimately how much the remaining cases are worth.
The first bellwether case went to trial earlier this year against Meta Platforms Inc. and Alphabet Inc.’s Google. A 20-year-old woman was awarded $6 million after a jury found the companies were negligent in the design and operation of their platforms and should have warned that their products could harm young users. Snap and TikTok reached confidential settlement agreements with the woman before that trial.

By all accounts, it was a perfect day to go for a run.
On the first Sunday morning in October 1972, Central Park was bathed in early fall sunshine, the crisp 50-degree air giving the changing leaves on the sugar maples and Sawtooth oaks near Tavern on the Green a bit of a sheen as the third New York City Marathon was scheduled to go off. It doesn’t feel right using an uppercase M with this marathon. At the time, the race was decidedly small-scale. Only 278 runners had signed up (for this year’s race on November 4, some 47,000 have entered), they paid just $1 to get in (instead of today’s $255), and the entire 26.2-mile race took place within the confines of the park, whereas today’s marathon stretches over five boroughs and requires the space of Central Park just to stage the start. And Fred Lebow, who would ultimately become the impresario of the world’s largest race, had yet to make a name for himself beyond the city’s small and chummy running fraternity.
But perhaps suggestive of his P.T. Barnum–like skills, Lebow had persuaded The New York Times and a few other dailies to come to the park that day. News, Lebow promised, would happen. So the Times sent one of its reporters, Gerald Eskenazi, to cover the race, and Patrick Burns, a Times photographer for nearly 50 years, to shoot it.
And, as promised, something happened, without a single running step being taken.
Shortly before 11 a.m., the six women entered in the race—yes, just six—lined up at the start. Lebow and his fellow organizers had openly courted women when the first New York City Marathon was held in 1970, even going so far as to ignore rules put in place by the Amateur Athletic Union that barred women from marathon race courses. For years the AAU, the then-governing body of track and field and distance running and which sanctioned events such as marathons, had been intent on smothering a bubbling interest among women who wanted to run longer and race farther. It did so by disseminating unfounded “scientific” research (for instance, that women who ran more than a few miles risked infertility) and invoking confounding rules to keep women on the sidelines.
But soon after the second New York City Marathon, in the fall of 1971, the AAU relented, somewhat, on its stance: It ruled that “certain women” could take part in marathons, provided they either start their race 10 minutes before or after the men or on a different starting line. The rulings—imposed so women would run a “separate but equal” race from the men—were viewed by many runners of the day, female and male alike, as just the latest act of discrimination enacted by the AAU.
Five of the six women on the Central Park starting line came from either Manhattan or Long Island. Their running résumés varied to the extreme: One woman had won the Boston Marathon five months earlier; another rarely ran at all. The five were in their late 20s and early 30s, friends or acquaintances who typically met in the park for training runs or to pass time while their husbands or boyfriends raced. The sixth runner was a 17-year-old from the Jersey Shore who had just started college the month before and had little connection to the other five women.

Dear New York City,
Probably the most excruciating breath I’ve taken in my life was in Lenox Hill Hospital on East 77th Street. It was my first breath on Earth, and my lungs must have wondered what had hit them. Forty-three years later, it seemed fitting that I’d come back to you for another challenge to my lungs and body: my first marathon.
I have lots of memories of you, starting from those early years on Manhattan’s Upper East Side. Then there were holiday visits and sleepovers with my grandmother in Stuyvesant Town, special days in Dad’s office in Washington Heights, Mom’s gallery openings in the Village. There were the fits and starts of my early professional career when I lived in Brooklyn and then Alphabet City, using most of my paycheck for rent, the rest for food. And of course, after I moved away in my late 20s, when I’d see you a couple of times a month for work.
If I’m being honest, you’ve always been a bit of a headache and a challenge. Back when I was just starting out, I couldn’t tolerate your high prices and abrasive attitude, and your tendency to “never sleep.” Which is why I ditched you for a less exhausting life in the country. Even today, I stress out just thinking about seeing you.
But on an unseasonably warm November Sunday, NYC Marathon day, you challenged me more than ever before—and revealed a level of grit I didn’t know was in me.
On the Verrazzano Bridge, I was overcome with emotion at having made it to the starting line. Surrounded by scores of runners from all over the world, with the open waterway below and the iconic skyline in the distance, I felt like a part of something huge and meaningful. It literally brought tears to my eyes.
Running through Brooklyn, I was in a zone. I was able to stay on pace and hit the halfway mark in decent shape, so I forced a smile at the throngs of cheering spectators. I’ve never been one to smile during races, and even your generous Brooklynites couldn’t get me to light up a genuine grin.
Then came the 59th Street Bridge. Long Island City, with its dull stretches of low-slung warehouses, is perhaps one of your most charmless neighborhoods. Nothing against the spectators who did their best in the streets leading up to the bridge, but that endless, gradual incline in the eerie quiet with the wind blowing up off the East River is where I started to unravel.
The screaming wall of people on First Avenue did nothing to energize me. This is where I began to feel like perhaps a marathon is just too long a run to be considered a wise choice.
And, sorry. Even if the Bronx had welcomed me with confetti and a marching band, it wouldn’t have mattered. Once I got to the Willis Avenue Bridge, I regretted not bringing money or a MetroCard so I could duck out and just go home. With every step, my feet, my quads, my knees threatened imminent shutdown. Worse was the shivering that seemed to consume my whole body, like when you lie feverish in bed, begging for the Tylenol to kick in.
Harlem was a fleeting boost, lifting me up ever so briefly at Mile 22 with its gospel choir, its Jamaican ska, its salsa beat. New York, here is where you started to shine and where I started to believe in myself. Your Harlem spectators literally reached out their hands and told me, “You can do this” and “You look strong.” They warmed me with their smiles when my body was wracked with chills. They let me pet their Bernese Mountain Dog, a wagging gift of comfort when all I wanted was to curl up on the sidewalk.

Many runners think of the climbs as the toughest part of a hilly race. Uphills send your heart rate soaring and slow even the strongest runners to a grind, while descents offer a chance to catch your breath and let gravity do some of the work. But David Roche, ultramarathoner and coach to New York City Marathon women’s runner-up Jess McClain, says those easier-feeling downhills can come at a cost later in the race.
And Roche knows the importance of late-race performance, which is why he integrates strategies into his training to fight fatigue through long distances.
Take McClain’s finish in New York City as an example: She outkicked reigning champ Hellen Obiri just feet from the finish line to take second place by mere seconds, clocking 2:24:42 and becoming the first American woman to reach the podium in NYC since 2018.
Roche’s fatigue-fighting tactics take him even farther in his own races. The two-time Life Time Leadville 100 winner—and course record holder—covered the famously demanding trails in 15:12:30, averaging roughly 9:07 per mile. Yet he rarely relies on extremely long, arduous training runs to prepare for conquering late miles.
Instead, Roche uses downhill workouts to reproduce some of the muscular stress that can cause runners’ legs to fail in an endurance event. “Downhills are the gateway to fatigue resistance in these really long events,” Roche tells Runner’s World.
The best part is, you don’t have to be an elite like McClain or Roche to benefit from his advice. He shares how purposeful downhill training can help runners preserve their strength, form, and pace deep into a race. Plus, he offers his go-to workout to add to your buildup.
Why Downhill Training Is an Underrated Durability Booster
Running downhill may provide some relief to your cardiovascular system—by lowering your heart rate a bit as gravity naturally carries you downward—but it puts much more strain on your musculoskeletal system. To keep you from tumbling down the hill, the quads must repeatedly brake the body’s momentum.
Braking action involves eccentric contractions, meaning the muscles produce force while lengthening under load, Roche explains. Eccentric contractions occur during many activities—including simply walking down stairs—but running a lengthy descent can deliver thousands in succession, significantly increasing the load on your muscles.
When the body isn’t accustomed to the stress caused by downhill running, the aftermath can wreck you. Roche explains that while a runner may feel relatively normal after their first downhill running workout, they end up developing significant soreness within a day or two. “That feeling of, ‘Oh man, I have no quads right now,’ a few days later is also what happens to your quads in an ultra,” Roche says—and even a marathon.
The initial downhill running effort, however, also triggers an adaptation known as the repeated bout effect. A review published in 2024 on the subject describes the repeated bout effect as a form of skeletal-muscle memory in which the first eccentric challenge activates protective responses that make the muscle more resistant to damage than subsequent ones.

You’ve crossed the finish line, collected your medal, and celebrated a goal that once demanded months of early mornings and long runs. Now comes the less glamorous part of the marathon: recovery.
You might be eager to get back on the road—or perfectly happy to take a break. Either way, the days and weeks after a marathon deserve as much thought as the training that got you to the starting line in the first place.
Here’s how to decide how long to rest, recognize when you’re ready to return, and ease back into training so you can build toward your next goal feeling strong.
How to Determine How Long to Rest After a Marathon
Exactly when you return to running after a marathon depends on how the race went, your overall effort during it, and how you feel. Some experts recommend one day of recovery time for every mile raced—so 26 days of rest for marathoners. And some even recommend one day of rest for each kilometer raced, which would mean 42 days of recovery.
Don’t panic, though! The good news is that “rest” does not have to mean no running at all (though it can). It just means taking a break from high-intensity training such as speedwork or other races.
Remember, running a race at a submaximal effort is different than racing it at a high effort. But either way, there’s no exact formula to follow for recovery after a marathon, so the best guide is really tuning in and listening to your body.
At a minimum, take three to seven days completely off from running after a marathon. Sleep in, eat, and enjoy your accomplishment. After that, begin an active recovery program. Active recovery includes light exercise and can include some running, if you are not sore and feel mentally and physically ready to get back to it.
More specifically, “light” exercise means exercising at a low-intensity level, i.e., no more than 60 to 65 percent of your max heart rate for a relatively short duration, like less than 60 minutes. Activity actually helps you recover faster than inactivity because it promotes circulation. And good circulation delivers fresh oxygen and nutrients to muscles and carries away metabolic waste and, therefore, aids healing and recovery.
If you do want to clock miles, focus on recovery runs during this time—keeping the effort light and easy, meaning you should be able to have a conversation the entire time you’re running.
Signs You’re Recovering From Your Marathon
Your body will let you know when it wants to run again, and one message it will send is through soreness. Minimal soreness is a good sign because it means your body is recovering from the challenge, but it may take a few days to kick in.
Delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) typically follows most marathon efforts. The soreness results from microscopic muscle tissue damage, and the severity of it depends on your fitness level and the intensity of the effort relative to the training effort. The degree of soreness indicates the extent of muscle damage, and this will influence the duration of your recovery period.
In other words, the more soreness, the longer the recovery. (A lack of soreness indicates you were well prepared for the demands of your race, so good job with your training.) When the soreness subsides, that’s an indicator that you’re ready for action again.

An updated version of its online access agreement that takes effect Nov. 24 states, "You are responsible for properly and timely revoking any authorization provided to an AI Agent and taking any necessary further action to cease the AI Agent's activities. J&J’s dividend grew 5.7% a year from fiscal 2015 to fiscal 2025, from $2.95 a share to $5.14. By TIKR’s count, it has paid more per share for 24 fiscal years in a row. After April’s raise, it pays $1.34 a quarter, or $5.36 a year.

In a report Monday, BofA Global Research economists called a sustained correction in the AI trade "one of the larger risks to the US and global economy." A slowdown would hit growth directly through spending, and indirectly through the wealth effect — when falling stock prices make households feel poorer and spend less.
The warning follows a three-week stretch in which AI stocks lost about $5 trillion in market value. The Nasdaq 100 (^NDX) ended Friday about 9% below its Oct. 6 record, though stocks are rebounding early Monday.
AI isn't just a stock market story anymore. It's an economy story.
Investment in computers, other information-processing equipment, and software added more than 1 percentage point to third quarter GDP growth of 3.4%, according to Yahoo Finance calculations using Bureau of Economic Analysis data. That's about a third of the total. In two quarters of 2025, it added more than the whole economy grew.
There's a silver lining. BofA's economists say growth now reaches well beyond AI. Without AI-related spending, the economy grew more than 2% last quarter, up from about 1% at the start of the year.
Stocks have never been a bigger share of Americans' savings
Chances are your 401(k) is in on the AI trade, too. Stocks made up a record 48% of Americans' financial assets in the second quarter, according to Federal Reserve data going back to 1945. That tops the 39% peak of the dot-com bubble.
That wealth is lopsided. The richest 10% of households own 88% of stocks, according to Federal Reserve data, so a lasting AI selloff would hit the biggest spenders hardest.
The pros aren't waiting around. Hedge funds are underweight the broader AI trade for the first time since early 2023, according to Morgan Stanley's prime brokerage data. That follows the biggest sustained cut to their stock exposure in its records.

It is awards season in Major League Baseball, and on Monday night, we learned the three finalists for each of the five major awards handed out by the Baseball Writers’ Association of America (BBWAA): Rookie of the Year, Manager of the Year, Relief Pitcher of the Year (a new addition in 2026), Cy Young and, of course, MVP.
All the finalists are deserving of course, but you can’t help but notice some names that might have fallen short.
When the award winners are announced next week, we’ll get the full totals and find out who received some of the down-ballot votes. But for now, we’d love to give a hat tip to a worthy player in each category who didn’t make the finalist cut.
Rookie of the Year: TJ Rumfield, Rockies
Yes, yes, I know: He’s a Rockie. Playing for the Rockies will always boost one’s offensive numbers at home, and that should always be taken into account. But Rumfield had some excellent numbers this year. Do you realize that he was the National League leader in OBP at .390? Getting on base is a pretty important thing in baseball, and it’s something that’s hard to do, whether you’re playing at elevation or not.
Rumfield is the first rookie to lead his league in OBP in 100 years. (And before you ask, he actually got on base at a higher clip on the road, .395, than at home.) I don’t know how you ignore a rookie who led his league in OBP.
AL finalists: Kevin McGonigle (DET), Parker Messick (CLE), Payton Tolle (BOS)
NL finalists: Carson Benge (NYM), Sal Stewart (CIN), JJ Wetherholt (STL)
Manager of the Year: Oliver Marmol, Cardinals
All right, I hear you: The Cardinals finished in fourth place and actually won one fewer game in 2026 than they did in 2025. But a statement like that strips out a lot of context. The Cardinals traded away Nolan Arenado, Sonny Gray, Brendan Donovan and Willson Contreras in the offseason and made it clear that the team was prioritizing the future more than the present.
And yet, the Cardinals were in the Wild Card chase all season; a 9-15 September, after they’d traded away Dustin May, JoJo Romero and Lars Nootbaar at the Deadline, was the only reason their record fell. The Cardinals also didn’t sacrifice any of their plans for the future, with 13 players making their MLB debuts, including three (JJ Wetherholt, Joshua Báez and Leo Bernal) who are going to be mainstays of the Cardinals’ lineup for a long time. Add that to huge steps forward from Jordan Walker and Alec Burleson, and it sure looks like Marmol has navigated this transition masterfully.
AL finalists: Kevin Cash (TB), Chad Tracy (BOS), Will Venable (CWS)
NL finalists: Don Mattingly (PHI), Pat Murphy (MIL), Walt Weiss (ATL)
Relief Pitcher of the Year: Josh Hader, Astros
It’s weird to think that anyone could forget about Josh Hader, no? This is a six-time All-Star who has been one of the most dominant and decorated closers of his era. Sure, Hader missed the first two months of the 2026 season, not making his debut until June 2. But did you see how great he was once he returned? In 45 appearances, he gave up exactly five earned runs. Five! The Astros weren’t necessarily the most electric team this year, so it was easy to miss just how good Hader was. He had a comically small 1.01 ERA and, while allotting for the fact that he only threw 44 2/3 innings, it is possible that 2026 was pound-for-pound the best season of his 10-year career.

On the eve of the midterm elections, there may be larger issues but none may approach the convergence of economic development, technology, politics, and local concerns quite like data centers.
Certainly, data centers have become a steady rallying cry in advertising and on soapboxes during various campaigns at all levels of government. In fact, some campaigns may have turned based on the stance candidates took on the issue. Some public officials may be ousted by the stance they have already taken.
Two well-known political strategists – David Axelrod and Karl Rove – weighed in on data centers at the annual meeting of the American Property Casualty Insurance Association in Boston.
“It’s a big issue,” said Axelrod, formerly chief strategist and senior advisor to former President Barack Obama. “It’s been a winning issue for people because they feel a loss of control. They feel that this is being done to them, and not with them.”
Axelrod acknowledged data centers are needed to accommodate the massive power demand artificial intelligence has required of critical infrastructure, but people need to feel they are participating in the process.
Without a lot of oversight from the federal level, governance of data centers will be done on a state-by-state basis, said Rove, former senior advisor and deputy chief of staff for former President George W. Bush. There will be winners and losers, but the winners will be the friendliest, which can be done while still keeping in mind the concerns and safety of constituents, he said.
Rove called out Texas Gov. Greg Abbott for putting a moratorium on data centers until developers demonstrate plans for water usage, power use and sharing capacity, local buy-in on locations, and property-tax obligations without the use of tax incentives.
“If you go around to all of the big boys in this business, they’ll say yes to every one of those,” Rove said. “And it is going to be a huge economic driver for the states that figure that out.”
“Everyone involved needs to be politically sensitive to why people are so resistant to it,” Axelrod added.
The pair of what many may consider unlikely friends also chimed in on AI – another hot-button issue that is not likely to be handcuffed by any regulation at the federal level.
“Nothing’s going to happen at the federal level the next two years,” Rove said. “If it doesn’t happen at the federal level, it’s not going to be industry-wide.” AI will evolve at lightning speed during the next two years of the administration so revisiting regulation after that may be difficult, he added.
The matter, therefore, will be left up to the states.
“I think that issue is so complex that it really cries out for presidents to be conveners of stakeholders to set rules of the road,” Axelrod said. “I think the president has put his thumb on the scale for the industry. I think going state by state is harder, but in the absence of federal leadership – and I don’t know that we’re going to get it for the next two years – I think you’re going to see states intervening in different ways.”

Extreme weather is having a measurable impact on Britain’s public finances as areas including railways, prisons and healthcare are increasingly affected, the UK’s National Audit Office said.
The full scale of the damage remains difficult to gauge, however, as many government departments are failing to provide the disclosures needed for a proper assessment, the NAO said in a report published on Monday.
“Parliament needs clear information on the resilience of infrastructure, service provision and finances to climate change, and on how these risks are being managed,” said Gareth Davies, head of the NAO, in a statement. “We expect this reporting to become more useful over time.”
This is the first year in which larger UK government departments have been required to publish the full details of the risks they face due to global warming. In many cases, efforts to understand such exposures remain at an early stage, the NAO said. Disclosures are necessary to help lawmakers keep track of how prepared the UK’s public services are, it said.
Britons are facing increasingly severe — and in some cases deadly — periods of extreme heat followed by flash floods. Intense heat has already resulted in damage to roads and railways, and left schools and hospitals dangerously hot this summer. At the same time, floods are becoming more frequent and more destructive to key infrastructure such as railways.
Flooding was the most common hazard identified in the disclosures monitored by the NAO. Some 89% of prisons face a high risk of flooding, while sites managed by the National Health Service saw 391 flooding incidents in 2024-25. Among the many impacts of overheating is the tendency toward more violence in prisons, the NAO report found.
“Government still has much to do, particularly in setting meaningful targets,” said Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, chair of the UK Parliament’s Committee of Public Accounts, commenting on the NAO’s findings. “Better reporting is encouraging, but Parliament and the public need more than a list of risks: they need to know how prepared government is to manage them.”

One year after Progressive insurance was forced to disgorge excessive profits in Florida, a Kemper insurance subsidiary must now do the same.
Infinity Auto, a nonstandard and specialty insurer based in Birmingham, Alabama, filed an excess profits report with the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation in June.
The OIR has “determined that Infinity has realized, and therefore owes to applicable policyholders, excessive profits in the amount of $46,246,666,” for 2023, 2024 and 2025 calendar years, reads an Oct. 22 order from Florida’s insurance commissioner.
Florida law provides a formula to be used to calculate an auto insurer’s underwriting profits: “Excessive profit has been realized if there has been an underwriting gain for the 3 most recent calendar-accident years combined which is greater than the anticipated underwriting profit plus 5 percent of earned premiums for those calendar-accident years,” the Florida law reads.
The OIR information did not indicate the number of policyholders who may see refunds or credits, nor what the average refunds will amount to. Checks should be mailed within the next two months. Commissioner Mike Yaworsky said Infinity Auto has agreed to try and locate any policyholders whose refund checks are returned. The company waived its right to an administrative hearing on the refund order.
“Kemper has taken a series of rate reductions for its Florida auto customers as insurance market conditions in the state have improved, following legislative reforms that reduced legal system abuse in Florida,” reads a statement from Kemper. “Relatedly, Kemper is returning approximately $46.2 million to eligible Florida auto policyholders through premium credits and refunds in accordance with Florida’s excess-profit provisions.”
The regurgitation order comes a year after Progressive was required to refund some $950 million in profits that were above the statutory formula’s threshold. That affected more than 2.7 million insureds and produced an average refund of about $300.
The announcement came just days after OIR announced an auto insurance rate cut by USAA insurance, and new homeowners rate decreases from 11 carriers.
More refunds for excessive profits are expected in the near future, OIR noted.

A federal judge dismissed on Monday a lawsuit by President Donald Trump’s administration seeking to force Harvard University to turn over records for an investigation into whether it continues to consider race in its student admissions process.
US District Judge Myong Joun in Boston rejected the US Department of Justice’s lawsuit, which Harvard contends was filed as part of a broader campaign by the Republican president’s administration against the Ivy League school.
The judge stressed that his decision rested on narrow, procedural grounds and did not resolve whether the Justice Department and US Department of Education could ultimately seek data on thousands of high school students who sought admission at Harvard.
But Joun, an appointee of Democratic President Joe Biden, agreed with Harvard that the Justice Department sued without taking all legally required steps aimed at securing the university’s voluntary compliance with its demands for applicant-level data.
“For example, the complaint does not allege that DOJ informed Harvard of the action it would take — namely, litigation — should Harvard fail to comply, nor does the complaint allege the specific failure identified,” Joun wrote.
The Justice Department and Harvard did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Harvard has been a top target of the administration’s effort to leverage federal funding and government power to force changes at universities that Trump says are dominated by “radical left” ideologies.
OTHER JUDGES RULED AGAINST ADMINISTRATION
The Cambridge, Massachusetts-based university has already secured rulings from other judges rejecting the administration’s efforts to terminate over $2 billion in grants, block the school from hosting international students and sue it for allegedly failing to protect Jewish and Israeli students from harassment.
The Justice Department filed the case before Joun in February, arguing Harvard was not complying with investigations into whether it is following the US Supreme Court’s 2023 ruling in a case involving the school rejecting race-conscious admissions programs used to boost enrollment of minority students.
The administration said it needed years of applicant-level admissions data to determine whether race remains a factor in Harvard’s admissions decisions and if the university is complying with Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which bars racial discrimination in education programs.
Data released by Harvard last week showed Black undergraduate enrollment fell for a third straight year since the Supreme Court barred race-conscious admissions, dropping to 9.3% in the class of 2030 from 11.5% in the class of 2029.
The university’s lawyers countered that the case was filed to retaliate against Harvard for refusing demands that it overhaul its governance, hiring and academic programs to align with the administration’s agenda.
They said the lawsuit was filed after Trump announced in early February that he was ending settlement talks and wanted $1 billion in damages from Harvard, which he said had “been, for a long time, behaving very badly.”
Joun, in dismissing the case on Monday, stressed that he was not resolving whether Harvard has discriminated or if it may ultimately be required to provide data to the agencies. The Justice Department could try to pursue a similar case again if it takes additional administrative steps, he said.
(Reporting by Nate Raymond in Boston; Editing by Sanjeev Miglani and Rod Nickel)

The New York State Department of Health said on Monday that a child in Lewis County had died in connection with an ongoing measles outbreak, marking the state’s first known measles-associated death in more than 30 years.
Last month, Governor Kathy Hochul declared a State Disaster Emergency in response to the measles outbreak across areas of New York and neighboring states.
“The Department has offered resources to Lewis County to assist with community outreach and support local vaccination efforts – both in response to this case, and as part of our ongoing efforts to support counties that are facing this ongoing measles outbreak,” the state department said.
The death comes as the US experiences its worst measles resurgence in decades.
Hochul told Reuters in October that the state would seek federal assistance to help contain the outbreak, but did not confirm whether it had submitted a formal request for a Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Epidemic Intelligence Service, or Epi-Aid, response.
As of October 24, New York had reported 178 measles cases this year, including 170 cases outside New York City and 8 cases in New York City.
State health officials said they were working with county health departments and local partners to provide measles, mumps and rubella vaccinations to unvaccinated individuals who request them and to investigate reported cases.
The US Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment outside business hours.
The CDC has recorded three measles-related deaths this year, but did not name the states where they occurred.
Pennsylvania has been the epicenter of the outbreak this year, reporting 1,433 confirmed cases and five measles-associated deaths so far this year.
The gap in numbers follows a policy shift under US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., with the CDC switching to the National Center for Health Statistics’ mortality data to track measles deaths, replacing its earlier reliance on state health departments’ figures.

Apple just made twice as much free cash as Microsoft, Meta, Alphabet and Amazon combined: Chart of the Day
Apple (AAPL) just had the biggest cash year in its history, and it didn't need to build a fleet of AI data centers to get there.
The iPhone maker generated about $136 billion in free cash flow — the cash left over after running the business and paying for buildings and equipment — in its fiscal year ended in September, according to its results Monday. That's up about 38% from a year earlier and well above its previous record of about $111 billion in 2022.
It's also roughly twice what Microsoft (MSFT), Meta (META), Alphabet (GOOGL) and Amazon (AMZN) made combined over their latest four quarters, by Yahoo Finance calculations.
The difference is the shopping list.
Those four companies spent more than $600 billion on capital expenditures over the past four quarters, much of it on AI chips and the data centers to house them. Apple spent about $9 billion in its fiscal year. That's down nearly 30% from a year earlier.
That bill is now showing up in their cash. Amazon has burned through about $42 billion over the past year, a record. Alphabet's free cash flow turned negative in the third quarter, and the stock just had its worst month ever. Meta's went negative for the first time since 2012.
Apple, meanwhile, brought in about $145 billion from its operations on record revenue of about $479 billion.
"We generated $28 billion in operating cash flow during the quarter, allowing us to return $28 billion to shareholders," CFO Kevan Parekh said in the release.
For the full year, Apple handed back about $102 billion through buybacks and dividends. Even that couldn't keep up, so the pile kept growing. Net cash — cash and investments minus debt — rose to about $57 billion from about $34 billion a year earlier.
The September quarter was the slow one. Operating cash flow came in slightly below a year ago.
Wall Street has noticed. Apple has become the market's hedge against the AI trade, and the stock was up about 25% this year through Nov. 2. Amazon, Microsoft, Meta and Alphabet ranged from a loss of about 11% to a gain of about 6%.
Apple isn't sitting out AI. Parekh said on the call that Apple will "significantly increase our overall investments in AI," mostly through research and development. He also said the cloud costs of running its new Siri will show up in what it spends to deliver its services. Asked whether Apple's spending was cooling after a heavy year, Ternus didn't budge. But at the same time, you can’t simply continue logging miles and workouts like you’re in race mode. Trying to stay razor-sharp year-round can lead to injury and burnout; your body needs rest after training for peak fitness.
So, instead, put your marathon fitness on ice. Freeze the adaptations you’ve gained and the endurance you’ve built. Then, you can pick up where you left off on, say, January 1, or whenever it’s time to lock back in for a spring marathon.
If you train right in the weeks between now and the new year, you won’t feel like you’re rebuilding fitness from scratch. Instead, you’ll preserve the key aerobic, muscular, and endurance adaptations you’ve worked so hard to develop.
To do that, we explain the minimum miles you need for maintenance and how speed, strength, and cross-training keep you in prime condition. Expect to return to race training feeling well-rested, confident, and ready to tackle another marathon cycle this spring.
How Many Miles Do I Need to Run Each Week?
In the first two weeks immediately following your marathon, you’ll want to focus more on rest and easy time-based jogging. Once you’ve recovered, however, you can return to tracking your miles more closely.
The bare minimum mileage you’ll need to maintain will vary from runner to runner, Heather Milton, CSCS, a clinical exercise physiologist and cofounder of Master My Run, tells Runner’s World. Much of it depends on how many miles you regularly put in over the weeks of your marathon training cycle.
“Science does not give us an exact number of what percentage of your marathon volume to decrease to that still allows you to maintain the same amount of aerobic fitness,” Milton explains. From her coaching experience, however, she’s found this number is likely around 50 percent of a runner’s typical weekly mileage.
David Hall, an RRCA- and USATF-certified run coach and founder of Running Coach CT, agrees. When planning his athletes’ schedules for the off-season, he looks at their typical running volume during marathon training and reduces their weekly mileage to no less than half. Every fourth week, however, mileage can drop to as low as 20 percent of their average to help facilitate recovery.
“A runner who was running 60 miles per week during their marathon build could definitely cut that in half,” Milton says. Or, take a runner who averaged around 40 miles per week. This individual could reduce their weekly mileage to 20, add in some cross-training, and expect to maintain much of their progress.
In fact, Milton adds, every runner can benefit from incorporating more of those cross-training sessions in the off-season. “Other forms of exercise can decrease the repetitiveness of the running motion and help you develop more well-rounded fitness, so I do prefer more variety from cross-training in the down-season,” she explains.
At the same time, Milton wants people to do the exercise they enjoy and, of course, runners love running. “I have to be reasonable about what a runner is willing to do and what keeps them healthy while they’re doing it,” she says. If you want to keep running four days per week in the off-season, that’s still workable—with one important caveat: You need to prioritize strength training.

Rachel Apa was nearing the end of her first New York City Marathon when she collapsed in Central Park on Sunday, November 1. The 24-year-old had spent months putting in the work needed to conquer 26.2 miles, but never made it across the finish line. Instead, she was taken to Mount Sinai Medical Center, where she died later that night.
Apa, a Bucknell University alum who lived in central Pennsylvania, came to New York to run with Parkinson's Foundation Champions, raising money in memory of her grandfather, who died from the disease in 2022.
According to reporting from The New York Times, the medical emergency happened around 1:30 p.m. close to Mile 24, around 85th Street, right as runners enter the final stretch through Central Park. Several spectators rushed to help and began performing CPR. New York Road Runners medical staff arrived shortly after, and tried to resuscitate her with a defibrillator before paramedics took her to the hospital.
Her parents had been keeping up with Rachel throughout the race as she made her way through the five boroughs, though from different locations. Michelle Apa, her mother, was in New York and watched Rachel run through Queens at Mile 14, while Steve Apa, her father, was back home in Lewisberry, Pennsylvania, following her progress through the marathon's tracking app.
Steve had been texting his daughter throughout the day. According to messages he shared with the Times, Rachel sent an "Ow" text at Mile 18, followed by a double "Ow ow" at Mile 19. She kept moving through the course, although her dad received no replies after that. As she reached Mile 23 on the app, Steve sent another message: "Final stretch." Rachel never responded.
Michelle eventually made her way to Central Park, reportedly arriving just as the ambulance carrying her daughter was leaving, per the Times. Doctors spent hours trying to save Rachel. Steve told the newspaper she was pronounced dead around 9:40 p.m.
"It's unfathomable," he told the newspaper. "Perfect health, perfect shape, 24 years old."
Steve told the Times that his daughter died from rhabdomyolysis, which occurs when damaged muscle tissue breaks down and releases substances into the bloodstream. The condition can cause serious kidney damage and, according to the Cleveland Clinic, can be triggered by extreme physical exertion.
An official cause of death had not been established as of Tuesday, November 3, with CBS New York reporting that the city's medical examiner was still investigating.
Sunday marked the marathon's first runner death following a medical incident since 2024, according to NYRR. The organization released a statement Monday:
"We are deeply saddened by the death of one of our runners following yesterday's race. Our thoughts and sincere sympathies are with the runner's family, friends, and the entire running community."

Both tobacco giants beat earnings estimates, raised their dividends, and surged more than 30% this year, but they pull retirees in opposite directions when it comes to income now versus income later.
Altria (NYSE:MO | MO Price Prediction) or Philip Morris International (NYSE:PM): which tobacco stock makes more sense for a retirement portfolio right now? Both companies beat third-quarter estimates, raised their dividends, and climbed sharply this year. Altria is up 37.87% year to date, and Philip Morris is up 31.41%. The choice comes down to a high-yield U.S. cash source against a lower-yield international compounder. They differ across income, growth, and valuation.
Income: Altria Pays Nearly Twice the Yield
Altria raised its dividend 4.7% in August to an annualized $4.44 per share. That was its 61st dividend increase in 57 years. At $75.82, the forward yield comes in at about 5.86%. Philip Morris raised its payout 8.8% to $6.40 annualized, its 19th consecutive annual increase. At $205.45, though, it yields only about 3.12%.
A similar margin covers each payout. Altria’s dividend equals roughly 78% of the low end of its raised 2026 adjusted EPS guidance of $5.66 to $5.74. Philip Morris pays out about 77% of the bottom of its $8.29 to $8.44 range. Altria has less leverage, with debt at 1.9x EBITDA. Philip Morris carries 2.17x net debt to adjusted EBITDA. Altria also added a $1B buyback expansion, while Philip Morris plans no buybacks in 2026. Winner: Altria.
Growth: Philip Morris Is Compounding Faster
Philip Morris expects adjusted EPS to grow 9.9%–11.9% this year and targets 9–11% annual EPS growth, excluding currency, through 2028. Smoke-free products now make up more than 40% of net revenue across 110 markets. VEEV shipments rose 61.6%, and the adjusted operating margin expanded 1.6 pts to 44.7%. The main near-term weak spot is U.S. ZYN, where management expects fourth-quarter adjusted operating income to come in at around zero or slightly negative as it invests heavily.
Altria guides to EPS growth of 4.5% to 6%. Its adjusted domestic cigarette volumes fell 4%, and Marlboro’s retail share slipped 1.0 pt to 39.5% as discount brands gained two share points. The company’s own chief executive said: “The consumer continues to be under economic pressure, no doubt.” Altria’s NJOY ACE vape is also off the U.S. market for now, and management has given no relaunch date. Winner: Philip Morris.
Valuation: Altria Trades at a Steep Discount
Altria trades at 13 times forward earnings. Philip Morris trades at 23. Enterprise value to EBITDA shows the same story: 12.59 for Altria against 19.01 for Philip Morris. The premium on Philip Morris prices in a lot of the growth already, and management has warned that full-year results will more likely land at the midpoint or lower half of guidance.
Analysts lean the other way. Altria’s consensus target of $73.45 is below its current price, while Philip Morris carries a $210.80 target and zero sell ratings. That shows how much Wall Street values Philip Morris’s growth. Still, for a buyer focused on what each dollar of earnings costs, Altria comes out ahead. Winner: Altria.

Its shares fell sharply following the announcement. But should investors be worried about the company's financial position, or is this simply the cost of building its next growth engine?
Here are three things investors should understand before making the next move.
Alphabet's free cash flow has turned negative
Perhaps the biggest concern from the latest earnings report is Alphabet's free cash flow.
The company generated $42.3 billion in operating cash flow during the third quarter. However, it spent $51.4 billion on capital expenditures, resulting in negative free cash flow of approximately $9.1 billion.
This is the second consecutive quarter of negative free cash flow, marking a significant change for a company historically known for generating substantial cash.
The main reason is its aggressive investment in AI infrastructure. Alphabet is building data centers, purchasing servers and networking equipment, and expanding its computing capacity to support growing demand for AI services.
However, there are other factors worth understanding. Alphabet is also building inventory for its custom Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) systems, which it sells to customers. This requires the company to purchase hardware before receiving payment. Additionally, it made a $5.2 billion payment related to a 2018 European Commission fine during the quarter. These factors further affected cash flow.
Importantly, Alphabet generated $179.6 billion in operating cash flow over the trailing 12 months, and trailing 12-month free cash flow remained positive at $19.7 billion thanks to strong cash generation in earlier periods. It also ended the quarter with $265.1 billion in cash and marketable securities, although this includes $90.4 billion of equity investments.
In other words, the company isn't facing an immediate liquidity problem. But investors should pay attention if heavy investments continue to consume more cash, further draining liquidity in the coming quarters.

Dive Brief:
- Bank of America and the Sustainable Markets Initiative, a nonprofit founded by King Charles III, have teamed up to launch a $40 million investment strategy designed to develop and scale nature and biodiversity solutions.
- The strategy, called the Lighthouse Initiative, went live on Sept. 23 and will be managed by French asset manager Eurazeo as part of its Future Industries III Fund, which invests in sustainable industries across the globe. Investments made through the new strategy will be tracked through Eurazeo’s impact framework, which includes a biodiversity footprint assessment, according to a Monday press release.
- Eurazeo, along with Bank of America, led the initial capital commitments, though the companies said the initiative has been structured to welcome investments from new partners over time.
Dive Insight:
The Lighthouse Initiative seeks to direct private capital towards nature-focused projects that remain underfunded today, per BofA and SMI. The bank and sustainable markets venture said the strategy will make minority investments in environmental projects and tech businesses globally and align with the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, an international agreement adopted in 2022 that has set a path to stop and reverse biodiversity loss.
